title: An economic assessment of the drivers of illicit trade
gist: Oxford Economics argues that routine above-inflation cigarette excise hikes create profit incentives for criminals to sell cheaper illicit cigarettes, with actual illicit market growth depending on criminal networks, enforcement, corruption and cultural acceptance. Once illicit trade becomes endemic it is very hard to reverse.

themes.theme: Excise tax hikes fuel illicit cigarettes

insights.claim: Above-inflation increases in cigarette excise duties have become common government policy in many jurisdictions.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Persistent real excise escalation is a structural headwind on legal tobacco volumes and a tailwind for illicit share.
insights.quote: above-inflation increases in cigarette excise duties have become common government policy

insights.claim: Higher cigarette excise duties, while intended to raise revenue and cut consumption, create an incentive for criminals to evade taxes and compliance costs and sell illicit cigarettes below legal prices to price-sensitive consumers.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Steep tax hikes can backfire, eroding both government tax receipts and legal tobacco makers' volumes via substitution to contraband.
insights.quote: they may also create an incentive for criminals to avoid the payment of taxes and regulatory compliance costs

insights.claim: The tax-and-compliance wedge lets illicit sellers earn sizeable profits while still undercutting legal cigarette prices.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: The wider the price gap from excise, the larger the illicit margin pool and the stronger the downtrading risk for legal brands.
insights.quote: enabling them to make sizeable profits whilst selling illicit cigarettes at lower prices than their legal counterparts

insights.claim: Whether tax-driven incentives actually grow the illicit cigarette market depends on organised criminal networks, enforcement resourcing and effectiveness, corruption, and cultural acceptance of illicit goods.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Assess illicit-trade risk per market by enforcement strength, corruption and criminal network presence, not just tax levels.
insights.quote: depends on a wide range of factors including the presence of organised criminal networks

insights.claim: Once illicit trade becomes endemic in a market, it is often very difficult to stop, implying hysteresis even if taxes are later moderated.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Illicit share losses for legal tobacco may be sticky and not reversible by later tax relief, a lasting volume and revenue risk.
insights.quote: once illicit trade is endemic in a market, it can often be very difficult to stop

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' assessment of illicit cigarette trade drivers combines a literature review with case studies of nine countries chosen for diverse geographies, regulatory environments and tax policy experiences.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Cross-country evidence base is useful for comparing how tax policy translates into illicit trade outcomes.
insights.locator: The report assesses the economic drivers
